facet_selection_reasoning: This selection focuses on the conceptual interpretation of confidence intervals. It combines the core goal of understanding CI as a long-run process for capturing population parameters (A4, A5) with the most frequent student errors: interpreting the confidence level as a probability for a specific interval (B15) and confusing the target of the interval as sample statistics rather than population parameters (B16).

item.stem: A marine biologist calculates a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight of adult green sea turtles based on a random sample of 50 turtles. The resulting interval is (110 kg, 130 kg). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this interval?

options.text: If we were to repeat the sampling process many times and compute a 95% confidence interval for each sample, approximately 95% of the resulting intervals would capture the true population mean weight.
options.rationale: This is the correct frequentist interpretation of a confidence level (A4) and correctly identifies that the interval is intended to capture the population parameter (A5).

options.text: There is a 95% probability that the true population mean weight of adult green sea turtles is between 110 kg and 130 kg.
options.rationale: This option incorrectly interprets the confidence level as a probability for a fixed parameter once the interval has been calculated (B15).

options.text: Approximately 95% of the individual turtles in the population have a weight that falls between 110 kg and 130 kg.
options.rationale: This option incorrectly suggests that the confidence interval describes the distribution of individual data points in the population rather than the population parameter (B16).

options.text: There is a 95% probability that the sample mean of another group of 50 turtles will fall between 110 kg and 130 kg.
options.rationale: This option incorrectly treats the confidence interval as a probability statement (B15) and wrongly targets a sample statistic (a future sample mean) instead of the population parameter (B16).

item.explanation: The item assesses the student's ability to distinguish between the frequentist interpretation of confidence levels (long-run behavior of intervals) and common misconceptions. Option 1 is correct as it identifies the parameter as the target (A5) and uses the frequentist definition (A4). Option 2 fails because it treats the interval as a probability for the parameter (B15). Option 3 fails because it treats the interval as a range for individual scores (B16). Option 4 fails because it combines a probability interpretation (B15) with an estimation of a sample statistic (B16).

judge_report.item_stem_preview: A marine biologist calculates a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight of adult green sea turtles based on a random sample of 50 turtles. The resulting interval is (110 kg, 130 kg). Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this interval?

option_assessments.reasoning: The option correctly interprets the confidence interval using the frequentist perspective of repeated sampling (A4) and correctly identifies the target of the estimation as the true population mean (A5).
The option interprets the confidence interval as a 95% probability of containing the true population parameter for this specific interval, which maps exactly to misconception B15.
This option claims the confidence interval captures individual data points (individual turtle weights) rather than the population parameter, which aligns with misconception B16.

This option treats the confidence interval as a probability statement (B15) and incorrectly suggests that the interval is estimating a sample statistic (the sample mean of a future group) rather than the population parameter (B16).
